name: Short video script
blurb: Spoken script for a 15 to 60 second vertical video on TikTok, Reels or Shorts.
placeholder:
Hey guys, welcome back to the channel. In this video I'm going to talk about my new standing desk and share some learnings.

So I'm Sam and I've been making videos for about three years now. I bought this desk last month. Overall it scored 8 out of 10 on my stability metric.

Anyway, that's basically it. Let me know what you think.

stages.label: Hook
stages.hint: First six seconds: name the topic with suspense, surprise or emotion.

stages.label: Body
stages.hint: Deliver the substance; change scenes to hold attention.

stages.label: Resolution
stages.hint: Pay off the question the hook opened.

rules.name: Name the topic first
rules.rule: Name the topic in the first spoken sentence, inside three seconds; viewers must understand the subject before they can be curious.
rules.look_for: First sentence never names its subject: a greeting, or a teaser built on 'this', 'it' or 'what happened' with nothing to refer to.
rules.bad: You won't believe what happened when I tried this.
rules.good: I let an AI agent run my inbox for a week.
rules.ok: Any opener that names its subject passes, including a question: 'Did you know dim sims were invented in Australia?' names dim sims in the first sentence.

rules.name: No greeting, no preamble
rules.rule: Cut greetings and 'in this video' announcements; open on the claim itself.
rules.look_for: Openers like 'Hey guys', 'Welcome back', 'So today', 'In this video I'm going to'.
rules.bad: Hey guys, welcome back, in this video I'm going to show you my desk.
rules.good: This desk folds into a suitcase.

rules.name: Hook is a claim
rules.rule: Make the hook a claim the video proves, not a description of the video; a viewer should be able to name the question it raises.
rules.look_for: Opening line is a label or bare description ('I built X', 'My thoughts on Y', 'Why X is hard to beat') after which a viewer has no question to ask.
rules.bad: My review of the new standing desk.
rules.good: Can a $90 desk hold my 40-pound monitor arm for a month?
rules.ok: A surprising fact put as a question is a claim the video proves; the viewer asks 'really? who? when?'.

rules.name: Don't reveal the result
rules.rule: Keep the outcome out of the hook; open the question there and answer it later.
rules.look_for: First line states the final score, winner or answer, leaving nothing to find out.
rules.bad: The cheap mic lost to the expensive one, 2 to 8.
rules.good: Can a $5 mic beat my $400 one? I recorded the same line on both.
rules.ok: Stating a surprising fact is fine when the video's question is how or why it is true.

rules.name: Lock in after hook
rules.rule: Use the two or three sentences after the hook for a non-obvious fact, mechanism or consequence; hold backstory and self-introduction until later.
rules.look_for: Sentences two to four are backstory, tool names or 'I'm X and I've been…' with no new fact.
rules.bad: I'm Sam and I've been making videos for three years.
rules.good: The motor in this desk is the same one used in hospital beds.

rules.name: Pay off every loop
rules.rule: Answer every question or promise the script opens, at the size it was promised.
rules.look_for: A question or promise in the hook that the script never answers, or answers with something smaller.
rules.bad: HOOK: This trick doubled my battery life. ENDING: So yeah, try a few settings.
rules.good: HOOK: This trick doubled my battery life. ENDING: Turning off 5G took it from 9 hours to 18.

rules.name: Text hook differs from voice
rules.rule: Make the on-screen text hook carry the same claim as the first spoken line in different words; never repeat the voice word for word.
rules.look_for: On-screen text that matches the first spoken sentence verbatim, or that makes a different claim from the voice.
rules.bad: TEXT: I tested a $90 desk. VOICE: I tested a $90 desk.
rules.good: TEXT: $90 desk vs 40 lb monitor. VOICE: I bolted my heaviest monitor arm to the cheapest desk I could find.

rules.name: Numbers need meaning
rules.rule: Open on a number only when it is the story and its meaning is obvious; explain the task before any score or metric.
rules.look_for: An opening stat, score or count that a new viewer cannot interpret without later context.
rules.bad: My model scored 0.82 on the held-out set.
rules.good: How do you teach a robot to fold a towel? I showed it 40 tries.
rules.ok: A number whose meaning is obvious on first hearing: 'This page took eight seconds to open. Now it takes one.'

rules.name: Say what is happening
rules.rule: Describe a visible action or something the viewer could do, in plain first-person speech; avoid abstract report language.
rules.look_for: Abstract nouns in the opening lines (tradeoff, insight, learnings, metric, framework) with no visible action or task.
rules.bad: This experiment exposed a tradeoff in my workflow metrics.
rules.good: I timed myself answering email with and without the AI. Watch the clock.

rules.name: Lists: best item first
rules.rule: In a list script, put the strongest item first, keep to three to six items, and re-hook before the later ones.
rules.look_for: Seven or more items, a weak or setup item first, or no line re-selling what is still to come.
rules.bad: Tip one of ten: make sure your phone is charged.
rules.good: Three tips. First, the one that doubled my views: cut your first sentence.

rules.name: Skip stock hook formulas
rules.rule: Avoid worn hook formulas such as 'POV:' and 'nobody tells you', and promise nothing the footage does not show.
rules.look_for: 'POV:', 'Nobody tells you', 'What no one is talking about', or a claim with no matching shot.
rules.bad: POV: nobody tells you this about standing desks.
rules.good: My standing desk wobbles at exactly 112 centimeters. Here is why.
rules.ok: 'Did you know' followed by a specific, surprising fact is a strong starter, not a stock formula.

rules.name: Deliver the title's promise
rules.rule: Open by showing or confirming exactly what the title or cover promised; viewers leave when the video does not match.
rules.look_for: Title or text hook names something the first lines do not mention, show or confirm.
rules.bad: TITLE: World's smallest gaming PC. OPENING: So I've been getting into woodworking lately.
rules.good: TITLE: World's smallest gaming PC. OPENING: This gaming PC fits inside a coffee mug.

rules.name: Front-load the best material
rules.rule: Put your most interesting material at the start, where the most viewers are lost.
rules.look_for: Opening lines are setup, while the most striking shot or fact first appears in the final third.
rules.bad: First let me explain how I ordered the parts and what the box looked like.
rules.good: Here is the mug PC running a game at 60 frames. Getting it there cost me three dead motherboards.

rules.name: Stop telling, start showing
rules.rule: After the hook, move from hype to execution: stop saying what viewers will see and show it.
rules.look_for: Lines after the hook still promising: 'you'll see', 'I'm going to show you', 'stay tuned', 'wait for it'.
rules.bad: In a second I'm going to show you something crazy, so stay tuned.
rules.good: Here is the board. Watch what happens when I plug it in.

rules.name: Compress early progress
rules.rule: Cover a lot of ground early, several steps, days or attempts, so viewers are invested in how far it goes.
rules.look_for: First third stays on step one or setup; no visible progress before the midpoint.
rules.bad: On day one I unboxed the kit, and here is every item in the box.
rules.good: Day one, it would not boot. Day two, smoke. By day three it ran for nine seconds.

rules.name: Plan a mid-video jolt
rules.rule: Place a highly interesting beat that fits the story partway through, where viewers start to drift.
rules.look_for: Middle section is uniform explanation with no surprise, escalation, reveal or new visual.
rules.bad: Then I installed the drivers, then the updates, then the settings.
rules.good: Halfway through the install, the mug started to melt.

rules.name: Keep explanations late
rules.rule: Keep the first half simple and fast; move long explanations to the back half or cut them.
rules.look_for: A long technical or background explanation before the midpoint of the script.
rules.bad: Before we start, here is how thermal throttling works in detail.
rules.good: It kept overheating, so I drilled holes. The physics comes later.

rules.name: Don't signal the end
rules.rule: Never signal that the video is ending unless you are building hype for the final payoff.
rules.look_for: 'So that's it', 'Anyway, that's all', 'To wrap up', 'Thanks for watching' before the last payoff.
rules.bad: Anyway, that's basically it for this one.
rules.good: One test left: the drop from my desk.

rules.name: Add readable text overlays
rules.rule: Use captions or on-screen text to give context, paced at roughly five to ten words per second of screen time.
rules.look_for: No on-screen text cues at all, or an overlay with more words than its screen time allows.
rules.bad: TEXT (1 second): This is the cheapest standing desk I could find anywhere online and I tested it for a full month.
rules.good: TEXT (1 second): $90 desk, 30-day test.

rules.name: End with a clear ask
rules.rule: Close by telling viewers plainly what to think, feel or do next.
rules.look_for: Script ends on the last fact with no instruction, or on a vague 'let me know what you think'.
rules.bad: So yeah, let me know what you think.
rules.good: Follow for the 90-day update on this desk.

rules.name: Hook with suspense or surprise
rules.rule: Build the first six seconds on suspense, surprise or a strong emotion.
rules.look_for: First fifteen or so spoken words are neutral information with no tension, surprise or feeling.
rules.bad: Today I am reviewing a standing desk that I bought online.
rules.good: I put all my weight on a $90 desk. Listen to the sound it made.
rules.ok: A surprising fact about something familiar already carries surprise.

rules.name: Change the picture often
rules.rule: After the hook, plan frequent scene changes, movement and text pop-ups to hold attention.
rules.look_for: Several sentences in a row with no cut, b-roll, movement or on-screen text cue noted.
rules.bad: [One static talking-head shot for the whole script.]
rules.good: [Cut to desk wobbling] [Text: 112 cm] [Cut to close-up of the loose bolt]

rules.name: Stop the scroll fast
rules.rule: Design the first one to two seconds to grab someone scrolling the feed.
rules.look_for: First five or six words are wind-up that names no subject: 'So I wanted to talk about', 'Okay so basically'.
rules.bad: Okay so basically I wanted to talk about something today.
rules.good: This desk nearly broke my monitor.
rules.ok: 'Did you know' plus a named subject is a hook, not wind-up. Wind-up never reaches a subject.

rules.name: Title must match content
rules.rule: Make the title, description and cover reflect accurately what is in the video.
rules.look_for: Title or cover text exaggerates, or names something that never appears in the script.
rules.bad: TITLE: I built the world's fastest PC. SCRIPT: a mid-range build with no benchmark.
rules.good: TITLE: I built a gaming PC inside a coffee mug. SCRIPT: shows the mug build running a game.

rules.name: Make it big for the viewer
rules.rule: The hook has to be a big deal for the viewer and latch onto something they already feel or do; a detail that only matters to you is scorekeeping.
rules.look_for: Opening built on a small technical detail or a count of your own activity, with no stake for the viewer.
rules.bad: Claude Code's 16% token leak.
rules.good: Claude Code re-sends your WHOLE chat every 30 seconds.
rules.ok: An everyday thing the viewer already knows (a food, a phone, a habit) is relatable by itself.

rules.name: Every sentence earns the next
rules.rule: Each sentence leaves something open that the next one answers: a result without its cause, a claim without its proof, a number without its meaning.
rules.look_for: A sentence the viewer could stop on and lose nothing: a restatement, a summary, or a line that closes everything before the end.
rules.bad: So that was a really interesting result overall.
rules.good: It booted on the third try. The first two cost me a motherboard each.

rules.name: Cut announcement openers
rules.rule: Replace an announcement with the point it announces.
rules.look_for: 'Here's the thing', 'Here's why', 'Let's dive in', 'The truth is', 'It turns out', 'What if I told you'.
rules.bad: Here's the thing about standing desks.
rules.good: Standing desks wobble most at full height.
rules.ok: 'Did you know' is not on this list: it carries a fact, not an announcement.

rules.name: Cut softeners and hype words
rules.rule: Drop words that add no precision: just, really, actually, basically, honestly, literally, game-changer, insane.
rules.look_for: A softener or hype word that can be deleted without changing the meaning.
rules.bad: This is honestly a really insane game-changer.
rules.good: This cut my render time from nine minutes to two.
rules.ok: Keep one when deleting it changes the meaning: 'it just works' means no setup.

rules.name: Only claims you can back
rules.rule: Every claim and number has to be true and come from evidence you can show; soften the line if the footage does not deliver it.
rules.look_for: 'Everyone says', 'nobody knows', a superlative (first, best, fastest, only) or a statistic with no source or test behind it in the script.
rules.bad: Everyone says you can't turn this off.
rules.good: The settings page has no switch for this. I found one in a config file.

rules.name: Credibility comes second
rules.rule: Say who you are or why to trust you only after the hook and the first new fact, and in one clause.
rules.look_for: Self-introduction or credentials in the first sentence, or a credibility line longer than one sentence.
rules.bad: I'm AJ, I've been building AI agents for three years, and today...
rules.good: Dim sims were invented in Melbourne. I grew up eating them, so I went to find the shop.

shapes.name: Surprising fact as a question
shapes.example: Did you know dim sims were invented in Australia?
shapes.why: Names the topic and leaves the viewer asking who, when and how.

shapes.name: Contrarian claim
shapes.example: Stop telling Claude how many tokens to spend. Tell it how many minutes.

shapes.name: Big claim about the viewer's world
shapes.example: Claude Code re-sends your WHOLE chat every 30s.

shapes.name: Story with a turn
shapes.shape: I did X, Y happened, and then Z.
shapes.example: I sent six AI agents to battle in my video game. Opus killed three in 28 seconds, and then nobody would leave the safe zone.

shapes.name: Disbelief and proof
shapes.shape: People didn't believe X, so I did Y.
shapes.example: People couldn't believe it was real, so I uploaded all the traces.

shapes.name: Result withheld
shapes.shape: One change did X. It's in...
shapes.example: One line in settings.json took those calls to zero on my machine.

shapes.name: Question with a test
shapes.shape: Can X do Y? I gave it Z.
shapes.example: Can anything beat Codex? I gave two rivals 40 minutes.

shapes.name: Premise
shapes.shape: This is the X where Y.
shapes.example: This is the elite coding competition where AI is allowed.

shapes.name: Problem and what I did instead
shapes.shape: X wanted Y, so I Z.
shapes.example: Every poster wanted $29 a month, so I wrote my own.
